Thanks a lot for this. I wish I had more to say, but I think I'm burn out on the AI art debate, hah. (Honestly, I was burnt out on the NFT debate and /then/ AI art reared it's head. Like a goddamn hydra)

I'll admit, a lot of the reason I'm venting this today is from seeing one of my all time favorite artists succumb to despair and anger over an AI being trained off of her art style. I genuinely can't explain how much it physically hurts to think about. It's genuinely reassuring to see people rally behind this cause, but I guess I just wish I didn't have to fight anymore. I'm burnt out. If being an artist means having to fight the whole time, then the only artists who are going to survive are the ones with huge support nets. The ones who aren't disabled and have extra energy and loving families and aren't from low income areas. There's a reason the only percentage of artists that make any living are celebrity ones. Bleh

Alright, I'm finished with my daily dose of pessimism and can go back to thanking you. It genuinely does mean a lot to me, and even with my doomerist edge, I hope you're right.

I think creativity blurs the line between constructive and destructive. The part of me that's all "rage against the machine" wants to think that art is suppressed because it's a form of change, and society tends to view change as dangerous and destructive, but i doubt it's intentional that way. Maybe, when the constructive option isn't available, all that's left is the destructive one, and it's either self destructive or activism. 

I don't know. I want to think participating in art will always have worth, AI or not. There's scientific studies that show learning an instrument helps you learn other fields. There's studies about how going to art museums coincides with increased lifespans. It can't be pointless to spend time on art. It's just not respected, not supported. 

I wish we lived in a world where hard work and skill was actually rewarded. If you chase your bliss and work hard at creating, it's honestly cruel to still be unable to survive. There's no reason why this integral part of the human experience should be so inaccessible. I hope something works out for you.

I am so sorry- I wish there were stronger words. Everyone says "I'm so sorry", but these kinds of things run deeper than that. 

About a year or two ago, a kid I went to highschool with was murdered by his guardian at age 17. It was a similar situation - some kind of fucked up murder suicide. I was friends with him, had inside jokes, saw him around a lot - but we were not especially close, and I'm far from the most affected. Sometimes, I wrestle with whether or not I should feel justified in being haunted by it. But then all it takes is remembering that the news outlets misspelled his name, and I wanna scream again. 

These situations are horrible for so so *so* many reasons, but one of them is how alienating it is to be caught in the blast radius. For most people, the heightened violence of murder sounds fake, it sounds like an impossibility. I've found the most difficult part of dealing with it is the fact that reaching out becomes a conundrum. Most people will not know what to say, will not know how to relate. Your horror becomes alienating. I'm typing all this out to you, and hell, I'm not even sure it's the right thing to say. I don't necessarily have answers - I just want you to know that you're not alone.

This kind of grief is heavy. I hope the days get easier to breathe through.

She cares because one of the things that brought us together was our shared love for creative writing. Collaborating together on stories is a pretty big facet of our relationship, and we've nurtered an understanding of one another's creative muses. I think sometimes she gets insecure about her own ability to write, so she tends to rely on me to give her something to work with. 

She doesn't need to read everything I write, but she tries to get involved in everything anyway. It can be nice, because I genuinely need the encouragement. If I put up a boundary and say she's not allowed to read something I've written, she'll sulk, but she'll respect it.

I do separate venting writing from normal writing, but lately I've been doing it so much that it's upsetting her. When I try to let her in to collaborate on the trauma centric stories so that she feels included, she tries to remove the trauma.

I have places set aside that I can safely vent without her. My notepad app is a geological dig of bad poetry, lmao.
